summary: Describes an approach to implementing the Z39.50 information retrieval standard over TCP/IP, as used by implementors at the time. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: How libraries' search systems talk to each other across the internet.

questions: how does z39.50 work over tcp/ip
subtitle: How libraries' search systems work together over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Z39.50 is a standard library information retrieval protocol designed for OSI networks, but libraries implementing it on the Internet chose to use TCP/IP instead, needing guidance on how to do so correctly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how Z39.50 can be layered directly over TCP/IP, mapping its protocol messages (APDUs) using ASN.1 and Basic Encoding Rules, with TCP port 210 designated for Z39.50 connections.
tldr.outcome: Multiple institutions successfully demonstrated interoperable Z39.50 implementations over TCP/IP through the Z39.50 Interoperability Testbed, establishing a de facto standard for library networking.

today: RFC 1729 is an Informational RFC documenting how Z39.50 was successfully deployed over TCP/IP rather than OSI. This approach has remained the standard for Z39.50 implementations on the Internet.

sections.title: Z39.50 and TCP/IP
sections.content:
Z39.50 is a US national standard protocol for computer-to-computer information retrieval originally designed to work over OSI networks. It was first adopted in 1988 and revised extensively in 1992. However, many libraries implementing Z39.50 chose to use TCP/IP directly rather than OSI. They made this choice because OSI implementations were large, complex and not widely available for all the computing platforms libraries used. They were concerned that the overhead of OSI upper layers would outweigh the functionality gained.

During 1991 to 1993, a group of institutions participated in the Z39.50 Interoperability Testbed (ZIT) under the Coalition for Networked Information. By mid-1993, multiple independent Z39.50 implementations were operational and able to interoperate across the Internet. This RFC documents the implementation decisions and agreements made by Z39.50 implementors working over TCP/IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Z39.50 is a system for searching library catalogs. Libraries wanted to use it over the Internet instead of a more complex system. This RFC explains how to do that correctly.

sections.title: How Messages Are Encoded
sections.content:
Z39.50 specifies its protocol messages (called Application Protocol Data Units or APDUs) using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). To send these messages over TCP/IP, implementations use the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) to convert the ASN.1 structures into a byte stream.

The key restriction for TCP/IP environments is that Z39.50 implementations must use direct references for EXTERNAL objects rather than indirect references. This is necessary because TCP/IP has no presentation layer to support indirect references. A valid Z39.50 message sent over TCP/IP would also be valid in an OSI environment, but not all byte streams valid in OSI are valid in TCP/IP environments. Implementations should tolerate indefinite length encodings and accept various BER features to ensure interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Z39.50 messages are written in a special format called ASN.1, and then turned into bytes using a standard encoding. TCP/IP has to use a simpler version of this because it does not have all the features that OSI has.

sections.title: Starting and Stopping Connections
sections.content:
In the Internet environment, TCP Port 210 has been assigned to Z39.50 by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. To initiate a Z39.50 connection, a client opens a TCP connection to port 210 on the server and immediately transmits a Z39.50 INIT APDU using BER encoding.

Implementors should be aware of the Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) system, which used an earlier version of Z39.50. WAIS clients look very different from Z39.50 Version 2 clients. The way to detect a WAIS client is to check if the first byte on the connection is an ASCII zero. Some implementations recognize WAIS clients and provide backwards compatibility by reverting to the older Z39.50 Version 1 protocol used in WAIS.
sections.plainLanguage: Libraries call each other on a specific phone number (TCP port 210) and start the conversation with an introduction message. They need to be ready for old-style library systems that speak an older version of the language.

sections.title: Service Mappings and Communication
sections.content:
Z39.50 services map onto TCP connection control. When a client finishes its interaction with a server, it initiates a TCP CLOSE to end the session. This maps directly to the Z39.50 RELEASE service.

For association abort, a TCP CLOSE or TCP ABORT on either side of the connection accomplishes the abort. Real-world implementations must be prepared to handle both kinds of termination since TCP implementations differ in whether they can distinguish a TCP reset from other events.

Data transmission is straightforward: the client and server simply map the Z39.50 P-DATA service to TCP transmit and receive operations. TCP expedited data is not used by Z39.50.
sections.plainLanguage: When libraries are done talking, one of them hangs up using normal TCP closing. This is simple and straightforward communication over Internet telephone lines.

sections.title: Contexts and Record Formats
sections.content:
When a TCP connection is established on port 210, both client and server assume the application context defined in the Z39.50 standard is in place. Implementations can expect the diagnostic set BIB-1 to be supported. However, because TCP/IP has no presentation layer negotiation mechanism, clients and servers must be cautious about using alternative attribute sets, diagnostic formats or other optional extensions unless there is prior agreement to support them.

Record syntaxes present a practical challenge. The server cannot guarantee that a client will understand alternative syntaxes if its preferred syntax is not available. Several proposals address this: Z39.50 Version 3 may include a list of prioritized preferred syntaxes instead of a single preference, or servers could return a diagnostic indicating that no suitable transfer syntax is available. Robust implementations should be prepared to handle unknown object identifiers and generate appropriate error messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to agree on what language they will use and what formats they will exchange. If they cannot agree on the client's first choice, the server can say 'I do not understand that format.'

sections.title: Interoperability Issues
sections.content: Z39.50 Version 3 will include an 'other' data field in each APDU to carry implementation-specific extensions to the protocol. Some implementations already use this field informally. Interoperable implementations should include code that at least ignores these extension fields rather than treating them as errors, even though the standard might technically say they should be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: New versions of Z39.50 may add extra features. Smart implementations accept these gracefully even if they do not understand them.
